opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it's something we've spent a lot of time thinking about at d-Matrix.

When you look at how AI is actually being deployed today, especially inference, customers don't really buy chips. They buy capability. They want to know: how many tokens per second can I serve, at what latency, for how many users, and what's it going to cost me in power and floor space? A single chip or even a single card doesn't answer that question. The rack does.

The rack has become the natural unit because that's where all the hard problems come together: compute, memory, networking, power delivery, cooling. If you optimize just the chip and ignore everything around it, you end up with a great component that underperforms in the real world. The bottlenecks move. Suddenly it's the interconnect, or it's memory bandwidth, or it's the fact that your data center can only deliver so many kilowatts per rack.

For inference in particular, models are getting bigger, context windows are getting longer, and you're increasingly running things like reasoning and agentic workloads that generate a lot of tokens. You can't fit those on one device anymore, so you have to scale out across many accelerators with very low-latency communication between them. Designing at the rack level lets you treat that whole system as one coherent inference engine rather than a pile of parts you hope will work together.

And from the customer's perspective, it simplifies everything. Data center operators plan in terms of racks and power envelopes. If we can hand them a rack that's pre-integrated, works within their existing air-cooled or liquid-cooled infrastructure, and delivers a predictable level of performance per watt and per dollar, that's something they can reason about and deploy quickly. It turns AI compute from a science project into something closer to a utility you can plug in.

So for us, the rack isn't just packaging. It's really the right abstraction for how AI is going to be consumed going forward.

r001.rationale: The response says data center operators plan in racks and power envelopes, and that a pre-integrated rack with predictable performance is something they can quickly reason about and deploy.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that for a long time the industry has talked about chips, and chips are what we build, so I love talking about chips. But when you actually sit down with a customer who's trying to deploy AI inference at scale, nobody buys a chip. Nobody even really buys a server. What they buy is capacity, and the natural unit of capacity in a data center today is a rack.

A rack is where all the real constraints show up at the same time. You have a fixed power envelope coming into that rack, you have a fixed amount of cooling you can pull out of it, you have a fixed physical footprint, and you have a networking budget for how those systems talk to each other and to the rest of the data center. So when a customer asks us, "How many tokens per second can I get, and what does it cost me," the honest answer has to be given at the rack level, because that's where power, performance, and cost all come together. If you quote a number at the chip level, you can make almost anything look good. At the rack level, you can't hide.

The other reason is that it maps to how people actually plan. When an enterprise or a cloud provider is building out, they're thinking in terms of megawatts and how many racks that megawatt supports. So if we can say, here's a rack, here's exactly how much power it draws, here's the throughput you get for your model at your latency target, and here's the cost per million tokens, they can plug that straight into their planning. It turns a very abstract conversation about architecture into something concrete they can procure and deploy.

And frankly, it's also how we've designed the product. We didn't start by asking how fast can we make a single chip. We started by asking what the best possible rack looks like for inference, and then worked backward to the chip, the card, the server, and the software. So the rack isn't just a convenient unit for the customer. It's the unit of design for us too.

r001.rationale: The response says customers plan in megawatts and racks, and that giving a rack’s power draw lets them plug it into their planning—communicating that rack-level deployment helps estimate power requirements.

astra-6.text:
When you’re deploying AI at scale, you’re really deploying a system. The accelerator matters, but so do the memory, the networking, the power delivery, and the cooling. A rack brings those pieces together into a unit that a customer can actually plan around.

Then the conversation becomes: How much useful work can I get out of this rack? How many tokens per second can I serve, at what latency, within my power budget? And what does that cost me? That’s much closer to the customer’s problem than comparing the peak performance of individual chips.

It also gives you a building block for scaling. If you understand the capacity and infrastructure requirements of one rack, you have a more concrete starting point for planning a larger deployment, including how those racks connect to each other.

r001.rationale: The response says a rack helps customers plan around power and evaluate work within a power budget, but it does not clearly say that expressing deployment in racks lets them quickly estimate the deployment’s power requirements.

sol-6.1.text:
Because a rack is where compute becomes a deployable system. You can talk about the performance of an individual chip, but customers ultimately need to know how much work they can get done within a power, cooling, and space budget. That means looking at the processors, memory, networking, and how those pieces work together.

Thinking at the rack level brings those tradeoffs into focus. How much throughput can I deliver? How much power does it take? What does it cost to run? And if I need more capacity, how easily can I add another rack? It gives customers a practical building block for planning a deployment, rather than asking them to translate a chip benchmark into a data center.

r001.rationale: The response says rack-level planning brings power needs into focus, but it does not communicate that this lets customers estimate those needs quickly.
